title: Canada's OSFI Lets Property Insurers Use Catastrophe Bonds to Cut Capital Requirements: Indemnity Triggers, Canadian Collateral and Prior Approval Required
summary: OSFI's regulatory notice, dated July 20, 2026 and effective immediately, treats natural catastrophe bonds as unregistered reinsurance with no margin requirement for federally regulated property and casualty insurers, provided the bond has an indemnity trigger, Canadian-held high-quality collateral and OSFI's prior approval.
description:
Canada's federal insurance regulator has opened a door for catastrophe bonds. In a regulatory notice on using natural catastrophe bonds in its Minimum Capital Test guideline, the Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions says it will allow federally regulated property and casualty insurers to treat these bonds as a form of reinsurance that can reduce the capital they must hold for insurance risk. The OSFI page carries the date July 20, 2026, and Canadian Underwriter reported the change on July 27. The notice says the changes take effect immediately. It applies to federally regulated property and casualty insurers and excludes mortgage insurers.

A catastrophe bond, or cat bond, is an insurance-linked security issued to transfer the risk of a defined natural hazard to investors in the capital markets. OSFI's definition covers securities issued solely to transfer natural-hazard risk for a predefined peril. The listed perils are earthquakes, hurricanes, severe convective storms, floods, wildfires and other naturally occurring environmental events. Man-made or human-initiated events are excluded, including terrorism, war, industrial accidents, pollution, nuclear events caused by human action and cyberattacks. Investors put up money that is held as collateral. If a defined catastrophe occurs and the bond is triggered, some or all of that money is used to pay the insurer, and otherwise it is returned to investors with interest.

The notice sets out the conditions for capital credit. A qualifying bond is classified as unregistered reinsurance, with no margin requirement. OSFI states: "We expect the natural catastrophe bond to have an indemnity trigger." An indemnity trigger means the payout depends on the sponsoring insurer's own actual losses, not on a separate index or physical measurement, and the notice does not address parametric triggers. The collateral must be invested in high-quality assets, must be subject to the capital requirements for unregistered reinsurance, must be located in Canada and must be fully paid in under a reinsurance security agreement. OSFI is firm on the consequence: "We will not recognize the natural catastrophe bond for capital purposes if these characteristics are not met."

Insurers cannot simply adopt the treatment. OSFI says: "We expect insurers to obtain our approval prior to using natural catastrophe bonds to reduce capital required for insurance risk." Applications go to the insurer's lead supervisor with the information in an appendix. The appendix has ten items: the structure of the reinsurance programme and how it fits the insurer's strategy, its reinsurance risk management policy and Guideline B-3; the cat bond reinsurance contract, including settlement, governing law, loss calculation and payment terms; offering documents and investor information; inter-company agreements, the reinsurance security agreement and a diagram of the structure; confirmation that a default will not trigger cross-defaults in the sponsor's other debt or derivative agreements; auditor, legal or other opinions; documentation for the special purpose vehicle or issuing trust; investment management guidelines and oversight; a description of the type and quality of capital in the security agreement; and stress-testing and modelling reports. OSFI does not set specific standards for the special purpose vehicle, basis risk or counterparties in the notice itself, and it does not set public disclosure requirements, although insurers must give OSFI the offering documents provided to investors.

The notice is a stopgap. OSFI says it expects to include these adjustments in the next version of the Minimum Capital Test guideline, at which point the notice will be rescinded.

The Insurance Bureau of Canada, quoted by Canadian Underwriter, said that qualifying cat bonds will generally be treated like traditional reinsurance for capital purposes, without the additional margin requirement that applies to traditional unregistered reinsurance. It said the change removes a potential regulatory disadvantage, but that the choice between cat bonds and traditional reinsurance will still depend on pricing, transaction costs, investor appetite and each insurer's own risk needs. It said insurers can report approved bonds under the existing framework while OSFI updates its forms, that it does not expect reporting to be a major barrier, and that it is too early to predict how much the change will alter market behaviour.

Existing use in Canada is limited. Canadian Underwriter reports that only one Canadian insurer, TD Insurance, has publicly announced a cat bond covering Canadian perils. Its first deal, MMIFS Re Ltd. Series 2025-1, was issued in early 2025 and provided $150 million of additional reinsurance capacity for earthquakes and severe convective storms. Its second, Series 2026-1, provides $115 million of aggregate protection on an indemnity and annual aggregate basis for a three-year term from January 9, 2026 to December 31, 2028, covering named storms, earthquakes, severe convective storms, winter storms and wildfires. The article does not provide total Canadian cat bond volumes or details of other sponsors.

The regulatory change also sits alongside a heavy agenda at OSFI, including a new Credit Risk Management guideline and its Annual Risk Outlook, though those are separate from this notice. The significance of this notice is narrower and practical: it replaces uncertainty about capital treatment with a defined, if demanding, approval route. Whether Canadian insurers use it will depend on cost and on how quickly OSFI approves applications. Readers should consult the OSFI notice for the full conditions and appendix.
source_name: OSFI regulatory notice on natural catastrophe bonds in the Minimum Capital Test guideline (July 2026) and Canadian Underwriter (July 27, 2026)
image_alt: Storm-damaged property representing catastrophe risk transfer (illustrative)
key_points: OSFI's regulatory notice, dated July 20, 2026 on the page and effective immediately, allows federally regulated property and casualty insurers, excluding mortgage insurers, to count natural catastrophe bonds as reinsurance that reduces insurance risk capital, subject to OSFI approval.

A qualifying bond is treated as unregistered reinsurance with no margin requirement; OSFI expects an indemnity trigger, and collateral must be invested in high-quality assets, held in Canada and fully paid in under a reinsurance security agreement.

OSFI says it will not recognise a bond for capital purposes if these characteristics are not met, and insurers must obtain its approval first by applying to their lead supervisor with a ten-item appendix covering the contract, offering documents, structure, collateral and stress-testing.

Covered perils are earthquakes, hurricanes, severe convective storms, floods, wildfires and other natural events; man-made events such as terrorism, war, cyberattacks, pollution and industrial accidents are excluded.

The Insurance Bureau of Canada said the change removes a potential regulatory disadvantage but that pricing, costs and investor appetite will still decide use; only one Canadian insurer, TD Insurance, has publicly announced cat bonds for Canadian perils.
why_it_matters: Catastrophe bonds move the risk of a major storm, quake or wildfire to capital-market investors instead of a reinsurer. Until now, Canadian regulatory capital rules did not give insurers clear credit for them, which made them harder to justify. The notice gives insurers a path to capital relief, but the conditions are strict and approval is required, so uptake will depend on whether the economics work. For homeowners and businesses, the benefit is indirect: a wider set of risk-transfer tools can help insurers keep offering cover in a market facing rising weather-related claims, but the notice does not itself change prices.

title: ASIC's Record 2025-26: $830 Million in Court-Ordered Penalties, Up Eightfold, and the Insurance Cases Behind the Warning to Insurers
summary: ASIC secured $830 million in court-ordered civil penalties and $644 million in consumer remediation in 2025-26, against $104.1 million in penalties the year before; insurance-related actions include the $23.5 million Cbus trustee penalty over claims delays and cases against Hollard and RACQ Insurance, and insurance complaints and claims handling remain a 2026 priority.
description:
The Australian Securities and Investments Commission has published enforcement figures for 2025-26 that dwarf the previous year's, and Insurance Business has set out what they mean for insurers. According to the figures published on July 20, 2026, ASIC secured $830 million in court-ordered civil penalties and $644 million in consumer remediation payments during the 2025-26 financial year. In 2024-25, it secured $104.1 million in civil penalties, so the latest total is roughly eight times as large. ASIC also reported 25 criminal convictions, more than 250 investigations, 32 civil proceedings and 18 criminal prosecutions.

The headline figure needs context. Insurance Business lists the largest penalties, and they are not insurance cases. Union Standard International Group was ordered to pay $300 million over misconduct involving contracts for difference, a single order that accounts for more than a third of the total. HSBC Bank Australia was ordered to pay $35 million over scam protection failures, with about $21.5 million in consumer compensation paid to date. Walker Stores was ordered to pay $33.5 million for unlawful credit practices that overcharged consumers by about $20 million. Westpac was ordered to pay $26 million over failures in responding to customer hardship requests, and Mercer Super $10.3 million for failing to report significant breaches to ASIC. The ASIC release itself does not contain the insurance cases below, which come from Insurance Business's account.

The most direct insurance-related penalty concerned a superannuation trustee. The Federal Court ordered United Super Pty Ltd, the trustee of Cbus, to pay $23.5 million over unreasonable delays affecting more than 7,000 members and claimants in processing death benefits and total and permanent disability insurance claims. Separate civil penalty proceedings against AustralianSuper, filed in March 2025 over alleged delays in processing death benefit claims, remain before the courts. For life insurers that provide group cover through superannuation funds, Insurance Business notes that such cases create compliance exposure that extends into service-level arrangements with trustees and does not sit with fund governance alone.

The coverage also lists actions against insurers and intermediaries filed in 2025. ASIC sued Hollard Insurance Partners Limited in April 2025, alleging that it breached its duty of utmost good faith by taking nearly three and a half years to resolve a storm damage claim from a couple in regional Victoria. In September 2025 it sued RACQ Insurance over more than 570,000 renewal documents that allegedly contained misleading "last period premium" representations over more than five years, despite customer complaints. It also sued Choosi Pty Ltd for allegedly misleading prospective customers through its funeral and life insurance comparison services. These are allegations, and the article does not report outcomes. In June 2025, ASIC reviewed the home insurer action plan across seven insurers, AAI Limited (Suncorp), Allianz Australia, Auto & General, Hollard Insurance Company, Insurance Australia Group, QBE Insurance and Youi, and found weak systemic oversight of independent expert reports and cash settlement fact sheets that offered minimal information on review rights.

ASIC has said where it is heading. Insurance Business reports that insurance complaints and claims handling are among its 2026 enforcement priorities, alongside private credit, financial reporting misconduct and misleading pricing. Sarah Court, in a November 2025 speech, described an environment "with premiums ever-increasing, claims rising, and insurance becoming increasingly out of reach," and said: "Where we see serious harm or risks to market integrity, we will act quickly." Death benefit claim volumes rose 10% in the twelve months to October 2025, and the regulator expects that growth to accelerate given Australia's ageing population.

The article draws several lessons for insurers. General insurers must notify ASIC within 30 calendar days of a reportable situation, and ASIC regards a failure to report as likely to be a significant breach in itself, as the Mercer Super penalty shows. The General Insurance Code of Practice contains financial hardship provisions comparable to those Westpac was penalised for breaching. The Australian Prudential Regulation Authority's 2025-26 corporate plan signals stronger supervision and a willingness to take formal enforcement action. The Financial Accountability Regime was extended to insurers and their licensed non-operating holding companies from March 15, 2025, adding individual accountability for senior executives.

The pattern across these cases is consistent: the alleged failures are about time and clarity, not about novel legal questions. A claim that takes years to resolve, a renewal notice that misstates the previous premium, or a breach that is not reported within the required window are all things an insurer can measure internally. That is why the coverage presents the figures as a warning: the regulator is choosing cases where the conduct is easy to describe to a court and the harm to consumers is easy to see. For policyholders, the practical point is that delays and unclear communication are not only service problems but can be breaches that carry penalties. For insurers, the sensible response is to look at how long claims take, what renewal letters say and whether breaches are reported on time. Because the totals are dominated by a few very large orders, and because the insurance cases are mostly still allegations, readers should treat this as a signal of regulatory direction and not as proof that insurance penalties rose eightfold.

why_it_matters: A regulator that has multiplied its court-ordered penalties eightfold in one year is signalling that it will pursue conduct cases to the end. For insurers, the specific risks are slow or poor claims handling, unclear renewal communications and failures to report problems to the regulator. For superannuation members and policyholders, the cases show which behaviours the courts are treating as breaches. The headline total is driven by a few very large penalties, notably a $300 million order unrelated to insurance, so it is not a measure of insurance penalties alone.
